title: How do Organisms Reproduce?
description: Grade 10 Biology: asexual reproduction (fission, budding, fragmentation, vegetative propagation), sexual reproduction in flowering plants, and human reproduction & health.

topics.title: Asexual Reproduction
topics.concept:
Reproduction is the life process by which living organisms produce new individuals of their own kind. It does not maintain the life of an individual, but it is essential for the continuation of the species. Reproduction also passes on the body design (DNA) from parents to offspring, and the small variations that arise are the basis of evolution.

In asexual reproduction, a single parent produces offspring without the formation or fusion of sex cells (gametes). The offspring are genetically almost identical to the parent. Its common methods are:

  • Fission — a unicellular organism splits into two (binary fission, e.g. Amoeba, bacteria) or many (multiple fission, e.g. Plasmodium).
  • Budding — a small outgrowth (bud) forms on the parent and detaches as a new individual, e.g. Hydra, yeast.
  • Fragmentation — the body breaks into pieces, each growing into a new organism, e.g. Spirogyra.
  • Regeneration — some organisms can grow back lost body parts or form whole new individuals from a piece, e.g. Planaria, Hydra.
  • Spore formation — structures (sporangia) produce tiny spores that grow into new organisms, e.g. Rhizopus (bread mould).
  • Vegetative propagation — new plants grow from vegetative parts (root, stem, leaf), e.g. potato (eyes on tubers), Bryophyllum (leaf), money plant (stem cutting). This is used by farmers and gardeners to grow many identical plants quickly.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the method of asexual reproduction in (a) Amoeba, (b) Hydra, (c) Rhizopus.
examples.solution:
Match each organism to its method.

  • (a) Amoeba — binary fission.
  • (b) Hydra — budding.
  • (c) Rhizopus — spore formation.
examples.answer: (a) Amoeba: binary fission; (b) Hydra: budding; (c) Rhizopus: spore formation.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is vegetative propagation? Give two advantages.
examples.solution:
It is reproduction from plant parts.

  • New plants grow from a vegetative part such as a root, stem or leaf.
  • Advantages: plants identical to the parent are produced, and they grow and flower faster than from seeds.
examples.answer: Growing new plants from a vegetative part (root/stem/leaf); advantages: identical plants and faster growth/flowering than from seed.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why are offspring produced by asexual reproduction almost identical to the parent?
examples.solution:
One parent supplies all the genetic material.

  • There is no fusion of gametes, so the offspring get a copy of the single parent's DNA.
  • Hence they are genetically nearly identical (with only tiny variations).
examples.answer: Because there is a single parent and no fusion of gametes, so offspring receive copies of the parent's DNA and are nearly identical.

recap:
• Reproduction continues the species and passes on DNA, with variations driving evolution.
  • Asexual reproduction: one parent, no gametes, nearly identical offspring.
  • Methods: fission (Amoeba), budding (Hydra/yeast), fragmentation (Spirogyra), regeneration (Planaria), spore formation (Rhizopus), vegetative propagation (potato, Bryophyllum).

quiz.q: Reproduction by which a bud develops and detaches to form a new individual, as in Hydra, is:
quiz.explanation: In budding, an outgrowth (bud) develops and separates as a new organism.

quiz.q: Growing new plants from the leaf of Bryophyllum is an example of:
quiz.explanation: New plants from vegetative parts (here, a leaf) is vegetative propagation.

topics.title: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
topics.concept:
In sexual reproduction, two parents are involved and offspring are formed by the fusion of male and female gametes. This mixing of genetic material creates more variation, which is useful for the survival and evolution of the species.

In flowering plants, the flower is the reproductive organ. Its parts are: sepals (protect the bud), petals (attract insects), the stamen (male part = anther + filament; the anther makes pollen grains) and the pistil/carpel (female part = stigma, style and ovary; the ovary contains ovules). A flower with both stamens and pistil is bisexual; one with only one is unisexual.

The steps are:

  • Pollination — the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma. Self-pollination occurs within the same flower; cross-pollination occurs between two flowers, often with the help of wind, water or insects.
  • Fertilisation — after pollination, a pollen grain grows a pollen tube down the style to the ovule, and the male gamete fuses with the female gamete (egg) to form a zygote.

After fertilisation, the ovule develops into a seed (containing the embryo) and the ovary develops into a fruit; the other flower parts usually fall off. When conditions are right, the seed germinates into a new plant.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the male and female reproductive parts of a flower and the gametes they produce.
examples.solution:
Identify the reproductive whorls.

  • Male: stamen (anther) → produces pollen grains (male gametes).
  • Female: pistil/carpel (ovary) → contains ovules with egg cells (female gametes).
examples.answer: Male: stamen, making pollen; female: pistil (carpel), with ovules containing egg cells.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is the difference between pollination and fertilisation?
examples.solution:
These are two separate steps.

  • Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma.
  • Fertilisation is the fusion of the male and female gametes to form a zygote (it occurs after pollination).
examples.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma; fertilisation is the fusion of male and female gametes to form a zygote.

examples.problem: Example 3: After fertilisation, what do (a) the ovule and (b) the ovary develop into?
examples.solution:
Recall what each part becomes.

  • (a) The ovule becomes the seed.
  • (b) The ovary becomes the fruit.
examples.answer: (a) The ovule develops into the seed; (b) the ovary develops into the fruit.

recap:
• Sexual reproduction: two parents, fusion of gametes, more variation.
  • Flower parts: sepals, petals, stamen (anther → pollen) and pistil (ovary → ovules).
  • Pollination (pollen → stigma) is followed by fertilisation (gametes fuse → zygote).
  • Ovule → seed; ovary → fruit.

quiz.q: The transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma is called:
quiz.explanation: Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma; fertilisation follows it.

quiz.q: After fertilisation, the ovary of a flower develops into the:
quiz.explanation: The ovary becomes the fruit, while the ovule becomes the seed.

topics.title: Reproduction in Human Beings and Reproductive Health
topics.concept:
Humans reproduce sexually, and reproductive ability begins at puberty (around 10–14 years), when the body matures and the sex organs become active. Changes at puberty (such as growth of body hair, voice change in boys, and the start of menstruation in girls) are brought about by the sex hormones — testosterone in males and oestrogen in females.

  • The male reproductive system includes the testes (make sperms, the male gametes, and testosterone), ducts (vas deferens), glands and the penis. Sperms are tiny, motile cells.
  • The female reproductive system includes the ovaries (make eggs/ova, the female gametes, and oestrogen), the oviducts (fallopian tubes), the uterus and the vagina.

Fertilisation takes place in the oviduct, where a sperm fuses with an egg to form a zygote. The zygote divides to form an embryo, which embeds in the wall of the uterus and develops into a baby; it gets nutrition from the mother through a special tissue called the placenta. If the egg is not fertilised, the thickened uterus lining breaks down and is shed with blood through the vagina — this monthly flow is called menstruation.

Reproductive health means taking care of the reproductive system. Contraception (family planning) helps couples space or limit children — methods include barrier methods (condoms), hormonal pills, and surgical methods. Some sexually transmitted infections (STIs), such as HIV/AIDS, can spread during sexual contact; barrier methods help prevent them. Good awareness and hygiene keep the reproductive system healthy.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the male and female gametes in humans and where each is produced.
examples.solution:
Recall the gametes and the gonads.

  • Male gamete: sperm, produced in the testes.
  • Female gamete: egg (ovum), produced in the ovaries.
examples.answer: Male gamete: sperm (made in the testes); female gamete: egg/ovum (made in the ovaries).

examples.problem: Example 2: Where does fertilisation occur in the human female, and what is formed?
examples.solution:
Fertilisation happens in a specific tube.

  • It occurs in the oviduct (fallopian tube).
  • A sperm fuses with an egg to form a zygote.
examples.answer: Fertilisation occurs in the oviduct (fallopian tube), forming a zygote.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is menstruation, and why does it occur?
examples.solution:
It is part of the monthly cycle when fertilisation does not happen.

  • If the egg is not fertilised, the thickened uterus lining is not needed.
  • It breaks down and is shed with blood through the vagina — this is menstruation.
examples.answer: Menstruation is the monthly shedding of the thickened uterus lining with blood, which occurs when the egg is not fertilised.

recap:
• Humans reproduce sexually; reproductive ability starts at puberty, driven by sex hormones (testosterone, oestrogen).
  • Male: testes make sperms; female: ovaries make eggs.
  • Fertilisation occurs in the oviduct → zygote → embryo embeds in the uterus; nourished by the placenta.
  • Unfertilised cycle → menstruation; contraception and hygiene support reproductive health and prevent STIs.

quiz.q: In humans, fertilisation normally takes place in the:
quiz.explanation: A sperm fuses with the egg in the oviduct to form a zygote.

quiz.q: The developing embryo gets nourishment from the mother through the:
quiz.explanation: The placenta supplies nutrition and oxygen from mother to embryo.

questions.q: Reproduction is essential for the:
questions.explanation: Reproduction is not needed to keep an individual alive but to continue the species.

questions.q: Asexual reproduction involves how many parents?
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction needs a single parent and no gametes.

questions.q: Amoeba reproduces by:
questions.explanation: Amoeba splits into two by binary fission.

questions.q: Hydra and yeast reproduce by:
questions.explanation: Hydra and yeast reproduce by budding.

questions.q: Bread mould (Rhizopus) reproduces asexually by:
questions.explanation: Rhizopus produces spores in sporangia for asexual reproduction.

questions.q: Growing a potato plant from the 'eyes' of a tuber is an example of:
questions.explanation: New plants from a vegetative part (tuber) is vegetative propagation.

questions.q: Sexual reproduction is important because it produces:
questions.explanation: Mixing of gametes creates variation, useful for survival and evolution.

questions.q: The male reproductive part of a flower is the:
questions.explanation: The stamen (anther + filament) is the male part, producing pollen.

questions.q: Pollen grains are produced in the ___ of a flower.
questions.explanation: The anther of the stamen produces pollen grains.

questions.q: The transfer of pollen from anther to stigma is:
questions.explanation: Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma.

questions.q: After fertilisation in a flower, the ovule develops into the:
questions.explanation: The ovule becomes the seed; the ovary becomes the fruit.

questions.q: The male gamete in humans is the:
questions.explanation: The sperm is the male gamete, produced in the testes.

questions.q: In humans, fertilisation takes place in the:
questions.explanation: Fertilisation occurs in the oviduct (fallopian tube).

questions.q: The embryo receives nourishment from the mother through the:
questions.explanation: The placenta supplies nutrients and oxygen to the developing embryo.

questions.q: Methods used to prevent unwanted pregnancy are called:
questions.explanation: Contraception methods help with family planning and can prevent some STIs.

questions.q: Plants grown by vegetative propagation are genetically identical to the parent. A practical advantage of this for a farmer growing bananas is that:
options: All plants reliably have the same desirable qualities
questions.explanation: Identical offspring keep the parent's good qualities (taste, yield) in every plant.

questions.q: Why does sexual reproduction give a species a better chance of surviving a changing environment than asexual reproduction?
options: It creates variation, so some offspring may cope with new conditions
questions.explanation: Variation from sexual reproduction means some individuals may survive new challenges, aiding evolution.

questions.q: A pollen grain landing on a stigma grows a pollen tube. The function of this tube is to:
options: Carry the male gamete down to the ovule for fertilisation
questions.explanation: The pollen tube delivers the male gamete to the ovule so fertilisation can occur.

questions.q: Both budding in Hydra and binary fission in Amoeba are asexual because in each case:
options: A single parent produces offspring without gamete fusion
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction has one parent and no fusion of gametes.

questions.q: If the egg released in a human menstrual cycle is fertilised, menstruation does NOT occur that month because:
options: The thickened uterus lining is needed to support the embryo
questions.explanation: On fertilisation, the uterus lining is retained to nourish the embryo, so it is not shed.

questions.q: Using a condom is recommended not only for contraception but also because it:
options: Helps prevent sexually transmitted infections like HIV/AIDS
questions.explanation: Barrier methods like condoms reduce the spread of STIs as well as preventing pregnancy.
